items.title: A Stock That Has Raised Its Dividend Every Year Since 1963 Just Hit a Record High. It Handed a Couple Living on the Checks a $67,000 Reason Not to Sell
items.summary: A beverage maker that has raised its dividend every year since 1963 closed Friday at a record high. For a retired couple living on 20,000 of its shares, Social Security and a cash reserve, the federal income tax bill is $0. Here is why selling a quarter of the position at the top would cost about $67,000.

items.title: 4 Durable Dividend Stocks Retirees Can Count On for Passive Income
items.summary: One company has raised its dividend through seven decades of recessions, yet it is not the only name retirees should trust. Each of these four payers faces a real risk that could test the check, and the safest one may surprise you.

items.title: Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Just Hit a Record High as Nvidia Sank. A 67-Year-Old Who Bought 1,000 Shares in 2016 Can Sell $106,000 of It This Year and Pay 0% on the Gain
items.summary: Berkshire Hathaway rose all five days and closed Friday at a record $592.94, up 3.9% in the week Nvidia lost its CEO and fell 12.7%. A 67-year-old who bought 1,000 Class B shares ten years ago at $157.93 holds $592,940 and a $435,010 gain in a stock that pays no dividend. Under 2026's 0% capital gains ceiling he can sell 179 shares, about $106,000, and owe nothing on the gain; the only cost is $2,075 of tax on Social Security that the sale makes taxable.

items.title: Coca-Cola and J&J Just Hit Record Highs. A 62-Year-Old Put $300,000 Into Them and Procter & Gamble in 2016. Here’s How Much the Now 72-Year-Old Gets Paid Every Single Month
items.summary: A 62-year-old split $300,000 across Johnson & Johnson, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola on Nov. 14, 2016. Ten years of dividend raises later, here is the monthly check at 72, the cash collected, what the shares are worth after Friday's record highs, the reinvested version, and the federal tax on the checks.
